title: Bodily and Mental Harm
thesis: Veterans Affairs Canada employees offered MAID to wounded veterans seeking PTSD treatment. Disabled Canadians like Roger Foley have been offered an assisted death in lieu of the home care they request. Article 6(b) prohibits causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of an identifiable group.

scenes.headline: Bodily and Mental Harm
scenes.subhead: Veterans Affairs Canada offered MAID to a wounded combat veteran. Roger Foley submitted his case to the International Criminal Court.

scenes.speaker: Hon. Lawrence MacAulay, Minister of Veterans Affairs
scenes.speaker_meta: Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs (ACVA), House of Commons, 2022-12-01
scenes.quote: It is completely unacceptable for any Veterans Affairs Canada employee to suggest medical assistance in dying to a veteran seeking treatment. We have confirmed at least four such incidents.

scenes.unit: VAC employees offered MAID to veterans
scenes.context: Veterans Affairs Canada confirmed multiple incidents in which a Service Agent suggested MAID to veterans — including a Canadian Forces combat veteran with PTSD who had asked for treatment, not death. Reported by Global News, CTV, and CBC; corroborated in ACVA committee testimony.

scenes.speaker: Roger Foley, applicant — Foley v. Victoria Hospital (London, ON)
scenes.speaker_meta: Submission to the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court, Article 15 communication, 2023
scenes.quote: I have been offered medical assistance in dying multiple times. I have not been offered the assisted home care I have been requesting for years. I am being coerced into death by the denial of life.

scenes.unit: ICC communication filed by Roger Foley
scenes.context: Roger Foley's evidence package was submitted to ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan KC under Rome Statute Article 15, alleging crimes against humanity and genocide against persons with disabilities in Canada.

scenes.headline: Why this satisfies Article 6(b)
scenes.body:
Article 6(b) prohibits causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of an identifiable group. Offering an assisted death to a person seeking PTSD treatment, or to a disabled patient seeking home care, is not a clerical mistake. It is the substitution of state-administered killing for state-funded care. The mental harm — to the recipient, to their family, to every disabled and ill Canadian who learns of these incidents — is severe and ongoing.

The pattern is documented in House of Commons committee testimony, in CBC and Global News reporting, and in a live communication to the International Criminal Court.
